txLifecycle.heading: Blockchain transaction flow — end to end
txLifecycle.intro: You met each stage separately in Fundamentals; here is the whole journey once. Ethereum follows the same flow with validators instead of miners.

stages.title: Wallet signs
stages.what: Your wallet builds the payment and signs it with your private key.

stages.title: Broadcast
stages.what: The signed transaction is handed to the handful of nodes your wallet is connected to.

stages.title: Relay & check
stages.what: Every node checks the signature and that the coins are unspent, then passes it on.

stages.title: Mempool
stages.what: Valid but unconfirmed — the transaction waits in a queue ranked by the fee it offers.

stages.title: Block proposal
stages.what: A miner (Bitcoin) or a chosen validator (Ethereum) bundles waiting transactions into a block.

stages.title: Block accepted
stages.what: The block is broadcast; every node re-checks it and adds it to its own copy of the chain.

stages.title: Confirmations
stages.what: Each new block on top makes rewriting yours more expensive — or, on Ethereum, formally final.

stages.title: Irreversible
stages.what: The payment is final for all practical purposes — the recipient can release the goods.

txLifecycle.keyPoint: Every blockchain payment makes the same journey; platforms differ in who proposes the block and how fast it becomes final.

handoff.heading: Mechanics done in Fundamentals §2 — today, Bitcoin as a platform
handoff.lead: You know how Bitcoin works. Today we ask a different question: what did its designers optimise for, what did they give up, and what does that make it good for in business?

lens.title: Architecture
lens.desc: Four layers — and what each one buys a business: reach, auditability, finality.
lens.question: Which of the four layers does your business actually touch?

lens.title: The Trilemma
lens.desc: No platform gets everything. Bitcoin chose security and decentralization — and lives with the consequences.
lens.question: Which corner of the triangle can your use case afford to lose?

lens.title: The app layer
lens.desc: What gets built on a chain that cannot run programs: payment channels, inscriptions, sidechains, staking.
lens.question: Where does an application live when the base chain stays minimal?

handoff.keyPoint: Same Bitcoin, different question: not how it works, but what it is for and what it costs.

architecture.heading: Bitcoin Architecture
architecture.subtitle: Four layers. Click a layer to see what it does.
architecture.emptyHint: ↑ Click a layer above to explore it

app.label: Application Layer
app.description: The user-facing layer. Wallets (Electrum, Ledger, Bitcoin Core), exchanges and explorers translate raw blockchain data into readable interfaces. They talk to the network via RPC calls to nodes.

p2p.label: Network Layer (P2P)
p2p.description: Nodes find each other using DNS seeds and a gossip protocol. Every unconfirmed transaction is broadcast peer-to-peer and held in each node's mempool until mined into a block.

consensus.label: Consensus Layer
consensus.sublabel: Proof of Work · who may add the next block
consensus.description: Proof of Work (Fundamentals §2): adding a block costs real electricity, so rewriting history costs more than it pays. For a business this layer is the security budget — and the reason blocks arrive every ~10 minutes, not every second.

data.label: Data Layer
data.description: Blocks chain together via hash pointers. Each block contains a Merkle root of its transactions, enabling lightweight SPV proofs. The UTXO set is the minimal state needed to validate new transactions.

dataVisual.title: Block chain — hash linking
dataVisual.caption: Each block header references the previous hash — altering any block breaks all subsequent blocks.

steps.label: Peers
steps.desc: Each relays to their own peers

consensusVisual.title: Consensus as a cost, not a puzzle
consensusVisual.body: You are not paying miners to process payments; you are paying them to make rewriting history unaffordable. The bigger the bill, the safer the record.

buys.label: What it buys
buys.text: Finality without a referee — nobody can be asked to reverse a payment.

buys.label: What it costs
buys.text: Slow blocks, limited throughput and a large energy bill carried by fees and new coins.

appVisual.title: Applications on Bitcoin
appVisual.caption: Apps communicate with the network via RPC calls to Bitcoin Core nodes (port 8332).

architecture.keyPoint: A business touches the app layer; the other three layers are what make the record trustworthy without a bank.

trilemma.heading: The Blockchain Trilemma
trilemma.subtitle: Every platform optimises for two of these three and pays for it on the third. Hover a platform to see what it chose.

bitcoin.name: Bitcoin
bitcoin.detail: Every full node validates every transaction. Layer 2 (Lightning Network) handles micropayments off-chain.

ethereum.name: Ethereum + L2
ethereum.detail: Rollups (Arbitrum, Optimism, zkSync) batch thousands of L2 transactions into a single L1 proof — inheriting Ethereum's security.

solana.name: Solana
solana.detail: High hardware requirements concentrate the validator set. The network has experienced multiple outages.

trilemma.keyPoint: Bitcoin chose security and decentralisation and paid with speed: good for settling high-value transfers, not for small retail payments.

apps.heading: Beyond payments — Bitcoin's app layer
apps.subtitle: For most of its life Bitcoin did one thing: send value. Since 2018 an application layer has grown around the base chain — first, the layers that scale payments.
apps.subtitleAssets: Newer and more contested: assets inscribed on satoshis, and BTC used as staking collateral for other networks.

items.title: Lightning Network
items.what: Two parties lock funds on-chain once, then pay each other instantly and almost free off-chain. Only opening and closing touch Bitcoin.
items.adoption: Strike · Cash App · Phoenix · Wallet of Satoshi · public capacity ~5,000 BTC · ~15,000 routing nodes.
items.limit: Liquidity must be pre-allocated, so payments can fail to route.

items.title: Ordinals · BRC-20 · Runes
items.what: Ordinals (2023) number every satoshi and let you attach data to it — images, text, tokens. BRC-20 and Runes (2024) built token systems on top.
items.adoption: Multi-billion-dollar secondary market in 2023–24 · activity cooled after the 2024 Halving.
items.limit: Contested — inscriptions bloat the chain and spike fees.

items.title: Bitcoin sidechains & rollups
items.what: Separate programmable chains pegged to BTC: Stacks (own language), Liquid (federation of exchanges), Rootstock (Ethereum-compatible).
items.adoption: Stacks holds modest DeFi TVL (~$100–200M) · Liquid moves funds between major exchanges · Rootstock hosts steady DeFi activity.
items.limit: Each has its own trust model (federation or merge-mining) and none inherits Bitcoin's security.

items.title: Bitcoin staking — Babylon
items.what: BTC holders lock coins to secure other proof-of-stake networks and earn yield — without wrapping or moving the BTC off Bitcoin.
items.adoption: ~$5B+ BTC staked by late 2024 · mainnet live · multiple PoS chains buying shared security.

apps.caveatBody: Bitcoin's app layer is contested inside the Bitcoin community. Purists want the base chain minimal ("digital gold"); builders want a settlement layer for richer apps. Both camps have legitimate concerns.
apps.keyPoint: Bitcoin's base layer stays deliberately simple; scaling happens around it, and each layer brings its own trust model.
apps.keyPointAssets: Inscriptions and BTC staking turn Bitcoin into a settlement layer for new assets — both are young, and both are contested.

bestFits.heading: Where Bitcoin wins
bestFits.subtitle: Bitcoin's design choices (fixed supply, limited scripting, Proof of Work) make it good at a narrow set of jobs and a poor fit for many others.

items.name: Store of Value / Digital Gold
items.why: Fixed 21M supply + 15+ years of uptime + PoW security make it the most credible scarce digital asset.
items.example: MicroStrategy holds 450k+ BTC as treasury · El Salvador national reserve · BlackRock IBIT ETF ($50B+ AUM).

items.name: Cross-border settlement
items.why: Censorship-resistant, no intermediary, available 24/7. Settles in minutes vs days for SWIFT.
items.example: Used in inflationary economies (Argentina, Venezuela, Turkey) as USD-adjacent settlement rails.

items.name: Micropayments via Lightning
items.why: L2 payment channels deliver instant, near-zero-fee payments without touching the base chain.
items.example: Strike, Cash App, Wallet of Satoshi · streaming sats per second for content (Fountain podcasts).

items.name: Strategic reserve asset
items.why: Verifiable scarcity and no issuing jurisdiction make it attractive as a neutral reserve.
items.example: US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve (2025) · sovereign wealth fund allocations · corporate treasury policies.

bestFits.notFitBody: smart contracts, DeFi or NFTs (use Ethereum or another programmable chain), high-volume retail payments on the base layer (use Lightning), private B2B consortia (use Fabric). Bitcoin is not a general-purpose computer.
bestFits.keyPoint: Bitcoin wins where neutrality and scarcity matter more than features: reserves, settlement, censorship-resistant value.

quizTrilemma.question: A payments app needs 5,000 transactions per second and must never go down. Which corner of the trilemma does Bitcoin give you least of — and what does that imply?
options: Security — Bitcoin's small blocks make it easy to attack, so the app should pick a chain with more validators.
Scalability — Bitcoin's base layer handles single-digit transactions per second, so the app must move payments to a Layer 2 like Lightning or pick a platform that made a different trade.
Decentralization — Bitcoin is run by a handful of mining pools, so the app should move to a consortium chain instead.
None — difficulty adjustment speeds blocks up when demand rises, so 5,000 tx/s is reachable on the base layer.
quizTrilemma.explanation: Bitcoin chose security and decentralization and paid with throughput: roughly 7 transactions per second on the base layer and 10-minute blocks. That is a design choice, not a bug. A high-volume app either batches payments off-chain on Lightning and settles on Bitcoin, or picks a platform that made a different trade — Ethereum rollups, or a permissioned chain when the participants are known. Difficulty adjustment only keeps blocks near 10 minutes; it never makes them faster.

quizFit.question: Which of these is Bitcoin actually the right tool for?
options: A retail loyalty-points programme run by one supermarket chain.
A decade-long treasury reserve that no government or company can freeze, inflate or reverse.
An in-game economy with thousands of micro-trades per minute.
Private invoices between four B2B partners who already know each other.
quizFit.explanation: Bitcoin wins where neutrality and scarcity matter more than features: a fixed supply, no issuer, and a security budget that makes rewriting history unaffordable — exactly what a long-term reserve needs. Loyalty points have one trusted issuer who must be able to change the rules — a database. A game economy needs fast, cheap, programmable trades — a smart-contract platform. Private B2B invoices need confidentiality between known parties — a permissioned chain (Section 3).

takeaways.title: Section 01 — Key Takeaways
items: Bitcoin is permissionless: anyone can join, nobody can be excluded, nobody can undo
Four layers (apps, network, consensus, data); a business touches the app layer, the rest make the record trustworthy
Every payment makes the same journey (sign, broadcast, queue, block, confirm); platforms differ in who proposes blocks and how fast they become final
Trilemma: Bitcoin chose security and decentralization and paid with throughput; speed lives on Lightning or another platform
Bitcoin's app layer (Lightning, inscriptions, sidechains, staking) lives around the chain, each piece with its own trust model
Wins: reserves, neutral settlement, censorship-resistant value. Loses: programmable logic, private data, high-volume retail
